title: Sharp asymptotic theory for Q-learning with \texttt{LD2Z} learning rate and its generalization
claim: Decaying to zero gets the fast early error drop of constant step-sizes and the low final error of polynomial decay.
layout: 2 line-plot panels side by side, right panel zoomed on late episodes
description: Two side-by-side line plots, both with Episode on the x-axis and the error ||Q − Q*||∞ on the y-axis. The left panel covers episodes 0 to 5000 and compares a blue polynomially decaying schedule with an orange LD2Z schedule. The orange curve drops almost vertically from about 9.5 to near zero within the first ~100 episodes, then stays flat and low. The blue curve falls slowly and is still around 0.7 at episode 5000. The right panel zooms in on episodes 2000 to 5000 and adds a green constant step-size curve. The blue curve stays high, between 1.4 and 0.7. The green curve is noisy and jagged, hovering around 0.1 with spikes up to about 0.3. The orange curve is the lowest and smoothest, shrinking toward zero at the end. Legends sit in the top right of each panel. The eye goes first to the orange cliff on the left.
caption: {Comparison between polynomially decaying ($\eta_t=0.05t^{-0.65}$), \ldtz ($\eta_t=0.05(1-t/n)$) and Constant ($\eta_t=0.05$) step-sizes}
abstract: Despite the sustained popularity of Q-learning as a practical tool for policy determination, a majority of relevant theoretical literature deals with either constant ($Î·_{t}\equiv Î·$) or polynomially decaying ($Î·_{t} = Î·t^{-Î±}$) learning schedules. However, it is well known that these choices suffer from either persistent bias or prohibitively slow convergence. In contrast, the recently proposed linear decay to zero (\texttt{LD2Z}: $Î·_{t,n}=Î·(1-t/n)$) schedule has shown appreciable empirical performance, but its theoretical and statistical properties remain largely unexplored, especially in the Q-learning setting. We address this gap in the literature by first considering a general class of power-law decay to zero (\texttt{PD2Z}-$Î½$: $Î·_{t,n}=Î·(1-t/n)^Î½$). Proceeding step-by-step, we present a sharp non-asymptotic error bound for Q-learning with \texttt{PD2Z}-$Î½$ schedule, which then is used to derive a central limit theory for a new \textit{tail} Polyak-Ruppert averaging estimator. Finally, we also provide a novel time-uniform Gaussian approximation (also known as \textit{strong invariance principle}) for the partial sum process of Q-learning iterates, which facilitates bootstrap-based inference. All our theoretical results are complemented by extensive numerical experiments. Beyond being new theoretical and statistical contributions to the Q-learning literature, our results definitively establish that \texttt{LD2Z} and in general \texttt{PD2Z}-$Î½$ achieve a best-of-both-worlds property: they inherit the rapid decay from initialization (characteristic of constant step-sizes) while retaining the asymptotic convergence guarantees (characteristic of polynomially decaying schedules). This dual advantage explains the empirical success of \texttt{LD2Z} while providing practical guidelines for inference through our results.
